title: Nakayama's lemma for a nilpotent ideal (surjectivity modulo I)
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq R$ a nilpotent ideal ($I^k=0$ for some $k\ge1$), and $u:N\to M$ a homomorphism of $R$-modules (no finiteness assumed on $N$ or $M$). If the induced map $N/IN\to M/IM$ is surjective, i.e. $M=u(N)+IM$, then $u$ is surjective. (Equivalently, parts (9)-(10) of the source: if $M=IM$ then $M=0$; if $N,N'\subseteq M$ are submodules with $M=N+IN'$, then $M=N$.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DV (label lemma-NAK, Nakayama's lemma), part (11); proof: 'Part (9) holds because if M = IM then M = I^nM for all n and I being nilpotent means I^n = 0 for some n; Parts (10), (11), and (12) follow from (9) by the arguments used above' (i.e. (11) from (10) applied to the submodules Im(N -> M) and M, (10) from (9) applied to M/N)

proof.text: First prove part (9) of the source. Let $Q$ be any $R$-module with $Q=IQ$. By induction on $n\geq 0$, $Q=I^nQ$: the case $n=0$ is immediate, and if $Q=I^nQ$, then $Q=IQ=I(I^nQ)=I^{n+1}Q$. Choose $k\geq1$ with $I^k=0$. Then $Q=I^kQ=0$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DV (label lemma-NAK), proof of part (9)

proof.text: Now let $L,L'\subseteq M$ be submodules with $M=L+IL'$. In the quotient $Q=M/L$, every class is represented by an element $l+\sum_j i_jx_j$ with $l\in L$, $i_j\in I$, and $x_j\in L'$, hence lies in $IQ$; conversely $IQ\subseteq Q$, so $Q=IQ$. Step 1 gives $Q=0$, and therefore $M=L$. This is part (10) of the source.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DV (label lemma-NAK), part (10) and the proof's reference to the quotient argument used for part (3)

proof.text: Apply Step 2 with $L=u(N)$ and $L'=M$. Surjectivity of $N/IN\to M/IM$ is equivalent to $M=u(N)+IM$, so Step 2 yields $M=u(N)$. Thus $u$ is surjective, proving part (11) and the stated result.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DV (label lemma-NAK), part (11) and the proof's reference to the image-submodule argument used for part (5)

proof_origin.place: Algebra, Lemma 00DV (label lemma-NAK), parts (9)-(11) and proof
